newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary parliament approves pension reform package.
newsitem.headline: Hungary parliament approves pension reform package.

text.p: The Hungarian parliament approved on Tuesday a package of bills on a drastic overhaul of the pension system from January 1, 1998.

The new regulation supplements the antiquated "pay-as-you-go" system operated by the social security pension fund with private funds from which employees will receive 25 percent of their pensions in the future.
"We can call these bills epoch-making for Hungary," Tibor Schwarcz of the senior ruling coalition member Socialists' (MSZP) parliamentary group told a news conference following the votes.
With the introduction of the new regulation, Hungary would be the first country in the region to overhaul its communist-era pension system. Poland plans to launch a similar reform in 1999.

The government said earlier that demographic changes were likely to make the current system unfinanceable over the long term and the introduction of private funds would also discourage currently widespread contribution payment evasion.
Originally the government wanted the private funds to have a one-third share, but decided against the higher proportion during a public discussion of the guidelines of the bills.

Hungary has been urged by the World Bank as well as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to reform the pension system so as to avoid the long-term risk of a sharp increase in budget deficits due to the gap in the social security budget.
Hungary also expects private pension funds to boost the long-term investments of domestic players in the country's fledgling capital markets.

Schwarcz said three-quarters of the pensions would continue to be paid from the social security pension fund, which would retain elements of redistribution to prevent large differences in pensions between social groups.
Part of the obligatory contributions will be paid into private funds and the employees will also be allowed to accumulate pension savings without the government-guaranteed system.
The government will cover the social security pension fund's deficit. The bill also adopted guarantees for the repayment of obligatory contributions placed with private funds.

Choosing a private pension fund will be obligatory for school-leavers who start work next year, while government experts said that people under 37 would benefit financially from using both tiers of the new system.
The Socialists and the junior ruling coalition member Free Democrats' (SZDSZ) voted in favour of the package, while opposition party MP's were mostly against or abstained.
Opposition People's Party (MDNP) member Erzsebet Pusztai told a news conference following the votes that the bills were pushed through parliamentary discussion too hurriedly.
"There will be serious problems when the bills take effect," she said. "Perhaps the Constitutional Court will have to examine them and the next few parliaments will need to make many adjustments."
Schwarcz said the opposition parties had had the chance to submit modifying proposals to the bills.
